title: SELECT INTO
description: Learn how to use SELECT INTO to copy a table structure and data into a new table.

data.text: The SELECT INTO statement creates a new table and inserts rows from a query into it. It is a quick way to copy a table's structure and data.

data.title: SELECT INTO Syntax
data.content: Creates a new destination table and copies rows from a source query.
data.code:
SELECT 
    select_list
INTO 
    destination
FROM 
    source
[WHERE condition]

data.text: You can use the WHERE clause to copy only rows that meet a condition. You can specify columns in the select list to copy only certain columns. Note that SELECT INTO does not copy constraints such as primary keys and indexes from the source table.
Copy a Table Within the Same Database
The following example creates a marketing schema and copies the sales.customers table into marketing.customers.

data.title: SELECT INTO Within Same Database
data.content: Creates the marketing schema and copies all customers into it.
data.code:
CREATE SCHEMA marketing;
GO

SELECT 
    *
INTO 
    marketing.customers
FROM 
    sales.customers;

data.text: Query the new table to verify the copy:

data.title: Verify the Copied Table
data.content: Queries the marketing.customers table to verify the copy.

data.alt: SQL Server SELECT INTO example 1 output showing copied customer data

data.text: You can also use SELECT INTO to copy data across databases. The following example copies customer data from the current database into a new TestDb database.

data.title: SELECT INTO Across Databases
data.content: Creates TestDb and copies California customers into it.
data.code:
CREATE DATABASE TestDb;
GO

SELECT    
    customer_id, 
    first_name, 
    last_name, 
    email
INTO 
    TestDb.dbo.customers
FROM     
    sales.customers
WHERE 
    state = 'CA';

data.text: Confirm that only the California customers were copied:

data.title: Verify Cross-Database Copy
data.content: Queries the TestDb.dbo.customers table and counts the rows by state.
data.code:
SELECT 
    state, 
    COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM 
    TestDb.dbo.customers
GROUP BY 
    state;

data.alt: SQL Server SELECT INTO example 2 output showing cross-database copied data

data.text: Because SELECT INTO copies only columns and data, the new table has no primary key, foreign keys, defaults, check constraints, or nonclustered indexes. Add them back explicitly when the copy is meant to stay around.

data.title: Add a primary key to the copied table
data.content: The copied table starts as a heap with no indexes. Adding a primary key creates a unique clustered index and enables efficient lookups.

data.title: SELECT INTO is minimally logged only in bulk-logged recovery
data.text: In the full recovery model, SELECT INTO is a fully logged operation and can generate a very large transaction log for big tables. It also takes schema modification locks on the destination. For large archival copies, consider batching the insert or using the Import and Export Wizard / bcp instead.

data.title: SELECT INTO Key Points
points: SELECT INTO creates a new table and copies data from a query into it.
Use the WHERE clause to filter which rows are copied.
Specify columns in the select list to copy only certain columns.
SELECT INTO does not copy constraints or indexes from the source table.
You can copy tables within the same database or across databases.
